content.p: For most of its history the Warlocks Motorcycle Club of Philadelphia was known to the public through police reports and prison sentences rather than through anything the club said about itself. Published accounts place its formation in 1967, in southwest Philadelphia and neighbouring Delaware County. Its members wear a red-and-white harpy patch. A Pennsylvania state commission described it, with the Pagans, as one of the two primary outlaw biker groups in the state.

The record is uneven. A state crime commission said in 1990 that the club had carved out a niche in the drug trade. A New Jersey police sergeant was shot dead in 1995 by a man JerseyMan Magazine identifies as a Warlock. And in 2020 the search for a missing musician led detectives to a 19th-century crypt in a closed Philadelphia cemetery, where two bodies lay. In 2023 a jury convicted one Warlocks member of murder in that case, and another had already pleaded guilty to a second killing.

The Warlocks of Philadelphia share a name with an unrelated club in Florida, which wears a phoenix rather than a harpy. A motorcycle-gear retailer's history of both clubs says that the two share no leadership, bylaws, patches or history, and that each disputes the other's claim to the name. The Pennsylvania club's own account, as that page reports it, is that Florida riders picked the name up on a visit to the Navy Yards in Philadelphia in the late 1960s. The Florida club says it chose the name on its own aboard a Navy carrier. That page notes that both accounts come from the clubs themselves and that no court has settled the question. Reports about "the Warlocks" often blend the two. Everything below concerns the Philadelphia club.
content.h2: A regional club in the commission's file
content.p: The Pennsylvania Crime Commission's 1990 report, which covered the 1980s, named four major outlaw motorcycle gangs in the state: the Warlocks, the Pagans, the Wheels of Soul and the Breed. It said the Warlocks and Pagans, both modelled on the Hells Angels, had been the most active throughout the decade. The Pagans, with about 300 members, were the larger. The commission put the Warlocks at about 150, centred on southeastern Pennsylvania and southern New Jersey, with chapters in Delaware County, the Lehigh Valley and Norristown area, Philadelphia and southern New Jersey.

The commission said the two clubs, long bitter rivals, now frequently cooperated in drug distribution, and that both had been heavily involved in methamphetamine trafficking in the early 1980s before adding cocaine. It listed Warlocks members among the state's drug-trafficking groups. It also recorded smaller details of the clubs' dealings with one another: at Daytona Bike Week in March 1990, it said, the presidents of the Warlocks' Chester and Philadelphia chapters were seen with a Pagans mother-club member. In another episode in Collingdale, Delaware County, the report said Warlocks and Pagans leaders met after a Warlocks member tried to push the Pagans out of the area, and agreed that the Pagans would deal with him personally if the Warlocks could not rein him in.
These are the commission's findings and characterisations from that decade. They are not convictions of the club as a whole.

One of the club's more infamous cases came in New Jersey. In 1995, Franklin Township police sergeant Ippolito "Lee" Gonzalez was shot in Franklinville while investigating a burglary. According to JerseyMan Magazine, the man who shot him was Robert "Mudman" Simon, a Warlocks member originally from Darby who the magazine says was believed to be one of the club's founders. Simon had been paroled only 11 weeks earlier, after more than 12 years in prison for the shooting murder of his young girlfriend, which the magazine said followed her refusal to have sex with several club members on his order.

Simon was sentenced to death for killing Gonzalez. He never faced execution: according to the same account, another death-row inmate stomped him to death in prison. Retired Upper Darby police superintendent Michael Chitwood, quoted by the magazine from an earlier Inquirer interview, called the Warlocks "violent predators".

Pennsylvania's attorney general, Tom Corbett, announced the break-up of what WFMZ-TV called a $9-million methamphetamine operation run from Berks County. Four people were arrested, with Michael Spadafora, 42, of Exeter Township identified as the ringleader. Corbett said agents seized 68 firearms, some fully automatic or fitted with silencers. According to the station's transcript of his news conference, he said investigators believed the ringleader's methamphetamine was distributed across Pennsylvania and had also been supplied to the Warlocks. The station's report does not describe any of the four people arrested as a Warlocks member.

A federal case in Philadelphia involved a Warlocks member directly. Prosecutors said Andrew Carr, of Upper Darby, was a member of the club's Chester chapter and worked as the "muscle" for a methamphetamine business, threatening violence to collect debts and wearing his Warlocks jacket while doing so. The business sold about $40,000 of methamphetamine a month in Philadelphia and Delaware County, according to the US Attorney's Office. A federal jury convicted Carr, then 59, of conspiracy to distribute 50 grams or more of methamphetamine in May 2016. In April 2017 Judge Eduardo C. Robreno sentenced him to 132 months in prison. Carr had directed an Upper Darby recreation gym until he was fired in 2013. By the time of sentencing, eight members or associates of the business had been convicted, six of them sentenced.

The case that put the club back in the headlines began with a missing person. Keith Palumbo, 36, a musician and tattoo-shop worker from Drexel Hill, was last seen on 6 February 2020 and reported missing four days later, according to JerseyMan Magazine. His family has said he was not a Warlocks member, though he knew many of them. The Inquirer, citing prosecutors in 2023, described him as a prospective member. Palumbo had told a relative that if he ever vanished, they should look in Mount Moriah Cemetery, a closed Southwest Philadelphia cemetery where the Warlocks had ties.

On 3 April 2020 detectives went to the Cain family vault, where the marble slab sat slightly ajar with fresh scratches at its base. Inside, wrapped in a carpet, lay Palumbo. Beside him was a second, badly decomposed body. A DNA test later identified it as David Rossillo Jr., 33, of Upper Darby, who had disappeared in December 2017. The identification was confirmed in August 2020.

Michael DeLuca, a childhood friend of Palumbo, had been arrested in Cheyenne, Wyoming, on 2 April 2020 on a gun charge. JerseyMan Magazine described him as the reputed president of a Warlocks chapter. According to prosecutors, Palumbo was shot at a Woodland Avenue house known as the Warlocks' headquarters. DeLuca, known as "Kaos", pleaded guilty in January 2023 to third-degree murder and was sentenced to 15 to 30 years.

Three people helped dispose of Palumbo's body, prosecutors said: Billy Gibson, Buck Evans and Donna Morelli. It was taken to Morelli's house on Trinity Street, which backed onto the cemetery, then placed in the crypt. Morelli was a member of the cemetery's board of directors. District Attorney Larry Krasner said she had been previously married to a former Warlocks president and, he said, became the club's de facto leader once he died in 2015. All three pleaded guilty and testified for the prosecution. Gibson and Evans received two years of probation. Morelli received a sentence of up to two years in prison. The Inquirer reported that she was later charged with two counts of witness intimidation over online posts about the other witnesses, a case that was still pending.

Michael DiMauro, of Secane, Delaware County, was arrested in September 2020 and charged with Rossillo's murder. An affidavit of probable cause, reported by the Inquirer at the time, said a witness who was not named told police that DiMauro had shot Rossillo in the cemetery, then asked for help opening a grave. The medical examiner found that Rossillo died from homicidal violence with multiple gunshot wounds. DiMauro represented himself at trial. In August 2023 a jury found him guilty on every count, among them first-degree murder, conspiracy and abuse of a corpse, plus hindering apprehension, tampering with evidence and gun offences. Prosecutors said he shot Rossillo four times in December 2017, tied a rope around his neck and dragged him by car to the crypt. Morelli had passed a note that read "TELL DIMAURO THEY FOUND DAVE. HE NEEDS TO RUN NOW".

First-degree murder carries a mandatory sentence of life without parole in Pennsylvania, and prosecutors said that was what they expected at a hearing later that month. The pages gathered here do not report the sentence itself.

The reason for the killings is not known. Assistant District Attorney Robert Wainwright said rumours had circulated that the two men had broken club rules, but nothing specific was substantiated. Everyone involved, including the victims, was using methamphetamine at the time, he said, but there was no sign they were trafficking drugs. Rossillo and Palumbo were prospective members, working towards full status, while the killers and those who disposed of the bodies were full members. Wainwright said members testified that the unwanted attention after the arrests had left the Philadelphia Warlocks largely disbanded. Krasner said the convictions should send a message that cold cases would be solved.
